Theropod. A diverse group of bipedal carnivorous dinosaurs characterized by hollow bones, three-toed feet, and powerful hind limbs optimized for running and hunting. Ranging from the chicken-sized Compsognathus to the apex predator Tyrannosaurus rex, theropods dominated terrestrial food chains throughout the Mesozoic. Theropods are not extinct; birds are living theropods, representing an evolutionary continuation of this remarkable lineage.

Theropods evolved during the Triassic period and dominated the Jurassic and Cretaceous as the primary large terrestrial carnivores until the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction approximately 66 million years ago.

Their locomotion was bipedal. Strong hind limbs supported the body, while forelimbs were short and powerful, bearing claws for grasping prey. The tail provided balance.

Hollow bones, called pneumatic bones, reduced weight while maintaining strength, facilitating the power-to-weight ratio necessary for predatory speed and agility.

Tyrannosaurus rex is the most famous theropod: approximately 12 meters long and about 9 tonnes, with a powerful bite force of roughly 12,000 newtons, it was the apex predator of the Late Cretaceous.

Smaller theropods like Velociraptor and Deinonychus were highly agile hunters. Pack-hunting behavior is inferred from trackways and nesting sites.

Many theropods, especially smaller species and juveniles, possessed feathers or feather-like structures for insulation or display, as revealed by fossil evidence.

Birds are theropods. The evolutionary transition is complete. Birds retain theropod skeletal features including hollow bones, three-toed feet modified into perches, and a wishbone, confirming descent from small theropod ancestors in the Jurassic.
